implementation_notes: A Kotlin service usually does not need an external control channel: a MutableSharedFlow<ControlCommand> (or a Channel for point-to-point commands) inside a CoroutineScope is the control bus, one collector dispatches commands to the component's internals, and a StateFlow<ComponentState> is the status half that a health endpoint or console reads. Lifecycle control is structured concurrency: cancelling the scope's children (coroutineContext.cancelChildren() or Job.cancel()) closes the channels, terminates collectors and replaces 'stop the worker' commands with a deterministic shutdown. JVM JMX stays available for external control (see the sibling variant) and is the right choice when the operator is not part of the application.
pitfalls: A MutableSharedFlow with no replay and no buffer drops or suspends: emit() can wait forever when no collector is active, so command entry points should use tryEmit with a bounded buffer and report rejection.
Cancellation is cooperative: a component that never checks isActive or blocks in a non-cancellable call (JDBC, Thread.sleep) ignores the stop command until that call returns.
Collectors must not launch unbounded child coroutines per command, or the 'stop' cancels the dispatcher while its children keep running.

variants.name: JMX MBeans from Kotlin (platform MBean server)
variants.idiom_name: StandardMBean over a Kotlin control interface registered in the platform MBeanServer
variants.implementation_notes: Kotlin runs on the JVM, so the platform MBean server is available unchanged: a Kotlin class implementing a control interface is wrapped in StandardMBean (or annotated with Spring's @ManagedResource/@ManagedOperation) and registered under an ObjectName, which makes status available as attributes and commands as operations to jconsole, JMX connectors and monitoring agents. This is the interoperability choice for a mixed JVM fleet; the coroutine variant is better when lifecycle is hierarchical and the operator is the application itself.
pitfalls: A Kotlin `var` in an MBean interface becomes a remotely writable attribute, which bypasses command validation; expose state as `val` and change it only through operations.
Nullability does not survive JMX: nullable Kotlin types can raise OpenDataException when the attribute is unset, so MBean interfaces should use non-null types or Optional wrappers.

Registering the MBean in a lifecycle-aware component is easy to forget, and a duplicate ObjectName fails with InstanceAlreadyExistsException - a silently swallowed exception means the component has no control surface at all.
